title: Tale of the Man of Khorasan His Son and His Tutor

full_text:
An affluent merchant of Khorasan entrusted his only son, Farhad, to an eminent tutor, saying: 'Instruct my son in all the sciences of the world, and spare no expense.'

For seven years, the tutor instructed the youth in astronomy, Greek logic, mathematics, and classical rhetoric. At the end of that time, the tutor brought the young man back to his father, boasting: 'Behold, your son is a master of all knowledge! He can debate philosophers and calculate the orbits of the stars.'

The father smiled, placed a simple brass ring in his closed fist, and said to his son: 'You who understand the stars, tell me what is hidden within my hand.'

The son closed his eyes, calculated the astrological alignments, and declared: 'Father, it is round, it has a hole in the center, and it is made of metal.'

The father marveled: 'Flawless! And what is the object?'

The youth thought for a moment and said: 'It must be a stone water-mill for grinding wheat!'

The father looked at his small closed fist, and then at the pedantic tutor with a sorrowful smile: 'Your logic can deduce that it is round and made of metal, yet your common sense fails to see that a water-mill cannot fit inside a human hand!

You have filled my son’s head with abstract formulas, but you have left him devoid of practical sense, observation, and humble reality.'

The father took his son to the agricultural fields, apprenticing him to honest builders and farmers, having learned that true education begins where abstract vanity ends.
moral: True education trains the heart in empathy and honor, not merely the head in theoretical vanity.
